questions.question: Epochs $0=T_0<T_1<T_2<\cdots$ cut time into cycles, $\alpha=\lim_{t\to\infty}N(t)/t$ is the epoch rate, $Z$ the long-run average reward per cycle and $R=\lim_{t\to\infty}R(t)/t$ the long-run reward rate of a nondecreasing cumulative reward $R(t)$. Which relation does the renewal reward theorem give when $0<\alpha<\infty$ and $Z$ exists?
options: $R=Z/\alpha$: the reward per cycle divided by the number of cycles per unit time
$R=\alpha Z$: the number of cycles per unit time multiplied by the reward per cycle
$R=Z$: every cycle earns $Z$ on average, so the cycle lengths play no role
$R(t)=N(t)\,Z$ holds exactly at every time $t\ge0$, not only in the limit

questions.question: In the renewal reward theorem the cumulative reward $R(t)$ is nondecreasing with $R(0)=0$, and epochs $0=T_0<T_1<T_2<\cdots$ split time into cycles. Which requirement does the theorem place on these epochs?
options: The gaps $T_k-T_{k-1}$ must be independent and identically distributed.
The epochs must be the arrival epochs of the jobs or customers in the system.
The epochs must tend to infinity and have a rate $\alpha=\lim_{t\to\infty}N(t)/t$ with $0<\alpha<\infty$.
The gaps $T_k-T_{k-1}$ must be exponential, so that the epochs form a Poisson process.

questions.question: The cycle lengths $X_k=T_k-T_{k-1}$ are i.i.d. and positive with finite mean $\mathbb{E}[X_1]$. What is the epoch rate $\alpha=\lim_{t\to\infty}N(t)/t$ with probability one?
options: $1/\mathbb{E}[X_1]$, the reciprocal of the mean cycle length
$\mathbb{E}[1/X_1]$, the mean of the reciprocal cycle lengths
$\mathbb{E}[X_1]$, the mean length of a cycle itself

questions.question: To obtain the long-run fraction of time a single server is busy from the renewal reward theorem, with $L(s)$ the number of jobs in the system at time $s$, which nondecreasing cumulative reward $R(t)$ should be used?
options: $D(t)$, the number of departures in the interval $(0,t]$
$\int_0^tL(s)\,\mathrm{d}s$, the area under the queue-length path
The number of arrivals in $(0,t]$ that find the server busy

questions.question: With epochs $0=T_0<T_1<T_2<\cdots$ and a nondecreasing cumulative reward $R(t)$ with $R(0)=0$, which expression is the reward $Z_k$ earned during the $k$th cycle $(T_{k-1},T_k]$?
options: $R(T_k)$, the reward collected up to the end of cycle $k$
$\frac{R(T_k)-R(T_{k-1})}{T_k-T_{k-1}}$, the reward per unit time in cycle $k$
$R(T_k)/k$, the average reward of the first $k$ cycles

questions.question: A machine fails on average once every $\mathbb{E}[X]=50$ hours, repairs take no time, and every repair costs $c=300$. What is the long-run repair cost per hour?

Jobs leave a single-server queue at long-run departure rate $\delta=3$ per hour, and the mean service time is $\mathbb{E}[S]=15$ minutes. Using departure epochs as cycle ends, what long-run fraction of time is the server busy?

A single server alternates between busy periods with mean length $\mathbb{E}[U]=6$ minutes and idle periods with mean length $\mathbb{E}[I]=4$ minutes. Taking one cycle to be a busy period plus the idle period after it, what long-run fraction of time is the server busy?
Maintenance cycles of a pump last $8$ days on average. Each cycle costs a fixed $32$ for the overhaul at its start plus $3$ per day while the cycle runs. What is the long-run cost per day?

Customers arrive at a kiosk on average once every $20$ minutes, and independently of everything else each customer spends $1$ euro with probability $0.7$ or $5$ euros with probability $0.3$. What is the long-run revenue per hour?

Epochs are $T_k=k$, so $\alpha=1$, and the cycle rewards $Z_k\ge0$ are arranged so that the averages $\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^nZ_k$ oscillate between about $\tfrac{2}{3}$ and $\tfrac{4}{3}$ forever. The cumulative reward $R(t)$ is nondecreasing with $R(0)=0$ and these increments. What does the renewal reward theorem imply about $R(t)/t$ as $t\to\infty$?
options: It has no limit, because $Z$ does not exist although $\alpha$ does
It converges to $1$, the midpoint of the two oscillation levels
It converges to $\tfrac{4}{3}$, because $R(t)$ is nondecreasing
It converges, but the theorem cannot identify the value of the limit

questions.question: In the proof of the renewal reward theorem, $N(t)$ counts the epochs in $(0,t]$, so $T_{N(t)}\le t<T_{N(t)+1}$, and $R(t)$ is nondecreasing with $R(0)=0$ and cycle rewards $Z_k=R(T_k)-R(T_{k-1})$. Which pair of bounds on $R(t)$ follows?
options: $N(t)\,Z\le R(t)\le\bigl(N(t)+1\bigr)Z$, with $Z$ the average reward per cycle

questions.question: For one rate-stable single-server queue with busy-time reward $R(t)=\int_0^t\mathbf{1}\{L(s)>0\}\,\mathrm{d}s$, analyst A uses departure epochs ($\alpha=\delta$, $Z=\mathbb{E}[S]$) and analyst B uses ends of busy periods ($\alpha=1/(\mathbb{E}[U]+\mathbb{E}[I])$, $Z=\mathbb{E}[U]$), with $U$ busy and $I$ idle periods. How do their long-run busy fractions compare?
options: B's value is smaller, because busy periods end less often than jobs depart
They agree only when service times are exponential, as in an $M/M/1$ queue
A obtains the load $\rho$, whereas B obtains the ratio $\mathbb{E}[U]/\mathbb{E}[I]$
They are equal, because $\lim R(t)/t$ depends on $R(t)$ only, not on the epochs

questions.question: Jobs arrive at a single server with a finite waiting room at rate $\lambda=10$ per hour; a fraction $0.25$ of them find the room full and are lost, and every admitted job is served. The mean service time is $\mathbb{E}[S]=0.06$ hours. What long-run fraction of time is the server busy?

Demand for an item is deterministic at $d=20$ units per day. Each time the stock reaches zero, an order of $Q=100$ units arrives instantly at cost $K=50$, and holding costs $h=0.1$ per unit per day. Taking order epochs as cycle ends, what is the long-run cost per day?

In an $M/G/1$ queue with arrival rate $\lambda=3$ per hour and mean service time $\mathbb{E}[S]=0.2$ hours, let $\rho=\lambda\,\mathbb{E}[S]$; busy periods have mean $\mathbb{E}[U]=\mathbb{E}[S]/(1-\rho)$ and idle periods mean $\mathbb{E}[I]=1/\lambda$. Taking the ends of busy periods as epochs, what is the epoch rate $\alpha$?

Let $T_k=k^2$ and $R(t)=t$, so $R(t)/t\to1$, while the cycle rewards $Z_k=T_k-T_{k-1}=2k-1$ have averages $\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^nZ_k=n\to\infty$. Why does this not contradict the renewal reward theorem?
options: The theorem needs bounded cycle rewards $Z_k$, which fails here
The cycle lengths are not i.i.d., which the theorem requires
The epochs are not arrival epochs of a queue, so $\alpha$ is undefined

questions.question: Let $T_k=k$, so $\alpha=1$, and for every $k\ge1$ let $R(t)$ rise linearly from $0$ at $t=k-1$ to $k$ at $t=k-\tfrac{1}{2}$ and fall linearly back to $0$ at $t=k$. Then every $Z_k=0$, so $\alpha Z=0$. What happens to $R(t)/t$ as $t\to\infty$?
options: It converges to $\alpha Z=0$, as the theorem predicts for every reward function
It converges to $1$, because the peaks of $R(t)$ dominate in the long run
It has no limit: it is $0$ at each $t=k$ and close to $1$ at each $t=k-\tfrac{1}{2}$
It tends to infinity, because the peak heights $k$ grow without bound

questions.question: A machine works for a mean of $40$ hours until it fails, and the repair then takes a mean of $10$ hours. Each repair costs a fixed $100$ plus $30$ per hour of repair time. Taking failure epochs as cycle ends, what is the long-run repair cost per hour?

Cycles are i.i.d.: with probability $\tfrac{3}{4}$ a cycle lasts $2$ hours and earns a reward of $2$, and with probability $\tfrac{1}{4}$ it lasts $10$ hours and earns $30$. What is the long-run reward per hour?
